newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccans vote to lay basis of wider democracy.
newsitem.headline: Moroccans vote to lay basis of wider democracy.

text.p: Moroccans were voting on Friday in local elections aimed at giving more powers to rural regions to improve living standards for their inhabitants, and at laying the basis for wider democracy in the North African country.

"The local councils from now on will form the base of the national pyramid of democracy," the independent le Quotidien magazine said, referring to planned reforms under a constitution approved in September 1996.

With King Hassan saying last year on television that he was "fed up" of vote-rigging charges, and personally pledging honest elections, opposition parties are going all out to try to change three decades of rule at all levels by pro-government parties.
In a sign of the authorities' pledged "transparency", voting stations for the first time in Morocco were using transparent clear plastic ballot boxes for Friday's vote.

Later this year, under the new constitution, the 1,547 local councils emerging from Friday's vote will select three-fifths of the members for a new Upper House of parliament. The country will then have two assemblies in place of the one 333-seat body.

"The importance of Friday's polls lies in the fact that future communal representatives will hold three-fifths of the Upper House," said Mohamed El Yazghi, a leading figure of the opposition Socialist Union of People's Forces (USFP).

Under planned decentralisation, regional councils will also have greater finance and power to push for development to end the disparity between town and country. This is reflected in higher illiteracy, poorer health and living standards for those living in the countryside -- about 50 percent of the 28 million population.
A trickle of early voters arrived shortly after polling booths opened at 8 a.m. (0800 GMT). They are due to close at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT) although local officials can extend the hours if necessary.
More than 100,000 Moroccans are standing for around 25,000 seats in the councils on which about 65 percent of seats were held by pro-government and centre-right parties after the 1992 ballot.

At Lycee Moulay Youssef voting station near the Royal Palace in Rabat, one early voter Fatima Hamdi, a teacher in her early 20s, said: "I decided to vote for the USFP because I want a real political change...My generation is fed up with right-wing parties running the councils since independence in 1956."
Another voter, Abla Idrissi, a veiled woman, said she voted for the old-guard Istiqlal party.
"I think this time everybody is ready for a change in people and policies in communal councils."
A total of 13 political parties, including five opposition groups and around 15,000 independent candidates, are competing in the 16 provinces, including four in the disputed Western Sahara.
Some 6,600 women are standing for election.
Malika, a 40-year-old woman teacher casting her vote early in Rabat, said: "I"ll vote for a woman. I expect her to be more honest."
